summary: Publishes the text of an old Internet Draft proposing a SIP Diversion header, which tells the called party who a call was diverted from and why. It was published for the historical record and as a reference for later informational RFCs. Its status is historic.

eli5.summary: When a phone call is forwarded, a note says who it was meant for first and why it came to you. This note is kept for history.

questions: why was a sip call diverted
what is the sip diversion header
how does sip convey call forwarding information
subtitle: A header to track where a call was forwarded from and why.

tldr.problem: In legacy telephone networks, redirection information helps services understand call routing history. SIP lacks a standard way to convey this information, making it hard to implement features like call forwarding and voicemail.
tldr.mechanism: The Diversion header carries the previous request address and a reason code (busy, no-answer, unconditional, etc.), passed through SIP proxies and user agents as calls are diverted to new endpoints.
tldr.outcome: This proposal was not adopted for standardization. RFC 3325 (Private Extensions) and RFC 4244 (Request History) became the standard solutions instead.

facts.label: Reason codes
facts.value: At least 10 values defined (busy, no-answer, unconditional, etc.)

today: RFC 5806 is Historic. The IETF chose not to standardize this approach. Instead, RFC 3325 (Private Extensions) and RFC 4244 (Request History Information) became the standard solutions for conveying diversion and history information in SIP networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Legacy telephone networks use ISDN and ISUP signaling to pass redirection information through the network. This information tells service providers and applications what happened to a call before it arrived. SIP, being a newer protocol, initially lacked an equivalent mechanism.

The Diversion header proposal extends SIP to let the called party learn who the call was diverted from and why. This is essential for features like Automatic Call Distribution (ACD) systems, third-party voicemail services, and call forwarding applications that need to customize their behavior based on where the call came from.
sections.eli5: Old phone systems had a way to say "this call came from Alice but got sent to you because she was busy." SIP didn't have that until this proposal.

sections.title: When and How the Diversion Header Is Used
sections.content:
The Diversion header is added when a SIP proxy server, redirect server, or user agent changes the ultimate endpoint that receives a call. It answers two critical questions for the recipient: (1) who was the call originally intended for, and (2) why was it diverted.

The header contains the previous Request-URI (the address before the change), a reason code such as user-busy, no-answer, unconditional, unavailable, or deflection, and optional fields like a counter, privacy setting, and screening indicator. The header is preserved as calls flow through multiple proxies, allowing services further down the chain to see the full history.

Diversion headers are not added for routine routing decisions like speed dial expansion, only for feature-driven diversions.
sections.eli5: When forwarding a call, you attach a label showing where it came from and why. Each service that sees it keeps the label attached, so the final recipient learns the whole story.

sections.title: Header Syntax and Parameters
sections.content:
The Diversion header syntax follows the SIP name-addr format, with a set of optional parameters. The reason parameter carries codes like user-busy, no-answer, unconditional, time-of-day, do-not-disturb, deflection, follow-me, out-of-service, and away.

Other parameters include counter (total diversions seen), limit (maximum allowed diversions), privacy (full, name, uri, or off), and screen (yes or no, indicating if the number was screened). Multiple Diversion headers can appear on a single request, with the topmost being the most recent diversion and the bottommost the original.
sections.eli5: The header is a simple address with tags that say why it was forwarded and how many times it bounced around.

sections.title: Behavior at Each SIP Element
sections.content:
Different SIP elements handle Diversion headers differently based on whether they recursively process 3xx responses or forward them upstream. A recursing proxy that internally forks new requests must add the Diversion header to each downstream INVITE. A non-recursing proxy that forwards 3xx responses upstream must include the Diversion header in the response.

User agents receiving 3xx responses with Diversion headers copy them into newly forked requests. When a UAS generates a 3xx, it adds a Diversion header with the incoming Request-URI and a reason code. Proxies never remove or modify existing Diversion headers; they only add new ones when their own feature causes a diversion.

This design ensures that the entire chain of diversions is preserved and available to all downstream recipients, enabling smarter routing and service logic.
sections.eli5: Each person or service that forwards a call adds its own note to the label but never erases earlier notes. This way, the final recipient sees the complete path the call took.

sections.title: Real-World Use Cases
sections.content:
Call forwarding features are a primary use case. When Bob's phone has Call Forward Unconditional enabled and a call arrives for him, the diverting entity adds a Diversion header stating reason=unconditional before routing to Carol. If Carol then forwards the call because she is busy, a second Diversion header is added with reason=user-busy, and both headers travel to the final destination.

Automatic Call Distribution (ACD) systems use Diversion headers to route calls to the right agent team. A night service company can read the original intended recipient and customize the greeting. Voicemail services use the Diversion header to determine whose mailbox to store the message in, since multiple users might have calls diverted to the same voicemail server.

The RFC includes detailed message flows showing both recursing and non-recursing proxy behaviors, multiple diversions, and mappings to legacy ISUP and ISDN systems used in traditional telephone networks.
sections.eli5: A pizza restaurant's after-hours calls go to a night service, which reads the Diversion header to know you called for pizza, not flowers, and greets you accordingly.
